clue.text: Saw dog restrained by lead?

indicators.note: something restrained by another is held within it, so the dog sits inside the lead

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for the metal lead
Rover is the stock name for a pet dog

explanation.surface: A dog-walker notices a hound held back on its lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a past tense and 'lead' like a dog's leash; 'Saw' is an old saying and 'lead' is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old maxim, a traditional saying of folk wisdom.

clue.text: English chemist accepts sulphur from French one

indicators.note: accepts means takes in, so the chemist holds the next letter

parts.note: William Prout was an English chemist known for Prout's hypothesis
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: A British scientist takes delivery of sulphur from a French counterpart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French one' seems to describe a source of sulphur but defines the novelist Marcel Proust, famous for In Search of Lost Time.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Proust was a celebrated French novelist, so he is a Frenchman.

clue.text: Away with pretentiousness? Right, in this country

parts.note: off means away, as in going off
side is an old British word for swagger or pretentious airs

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether leaving pomposity behind is correct in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: SIDE for airs is dated British slang; in Britain, where cars drive on the left, the offside of a vehicle is its right-hand side.
explanation.definitionFit: On a British vehicle the offside is the side nearer the middle of the road, the right.

clue.text: A strange literary device!

parts.note: recalls Longfellow's poem whose hero carries a banner with a strange device, its one-word Latin motto

explanation.surface: An odd technique used in writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'literary device' looks like a figure of speech, but it is the banner's device in Longfellow's poem of that title: 'A banner with the strange device'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin motto meaning higher still is the device inscribed on the banner in Longfellow's poem.

clue.text: American woman took care to appear liberal

parts.note: broad is American slang for a woman
minded means looked after or took care

explanation.surface: A woman from the States was careful to seem tolerant.
explanation.walkthrough: BROAD is dated American slang for a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Broad-minded means tolerant of other views, open and unprejudiced.

clue.text: Vehicle rejected by motoring club sales place

indicators.note: rejected suggests something sent back, so the two pieces together are read from the end

parts.note: the RAC is Britain's Royal Automobile Club
a mart is a market

explanation.surface: A car is turned away by a motoring organisation from a showroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns the whole run RACMART round, giving TRAMCAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A tramcar is a passenger vehicle running on rails in a street.

clue.text: Three or four points to settle by investigation

explanation.surface: A judge weighs a few points before reaching a verdict.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby a try scored three points, later four (now five).
explanation.definitionFit: A rugby try is a score worth several points; to try a case is to decide it judicially.

clue.text: Informal excuse from one supporting a party member

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece lies beneath, so the figure comes last

parts.note: Lib is short for a Liberal politician
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: An excuse given by someone backing a political colleague.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Informal' fits the loose everyday sense of the answer: any excuse, not only proof of being elsewhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially an alibi is any excuse, though strictly it is a plea of being elsewhere.

clue.text: Country house appears posh, after a couple of drinks

indicators.note: after places the posh letter behind the two drinks

parts.note: cha is a slang word for tea
tea is the second drink
U means upper class, from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U

explanation.surface: A grand residence looks smart after a pair of cocktails.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'couple of drinks' are the same drink twice, CHA and TEA; U for upper-class is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A chateau is a French castle or large country residence.

clue.text: Type of overhead beam made heretofore — he abandoned it

indicators.note: made suggests the letters are reshaped into something new

parts.note: the fodder taken as written
the two letters to be taken away

explanation.surface: A carpenter says a roof beam was crafted previously, then left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'he abandoned it' says HE is removed from HERETOFORE, and 'made' rearranges the remaining RETOFORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rooftree is the ridgepole, the horizontal beam along the top of a roof.

clue.text: Concerning smell of extremely ornamental plant

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the next word, its first and last letters

parts.note: a plant is an industrial works, a factory

explanation.surface: Asks about the scent given off by a very decorative plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks botanical but means an industrial works; OL is the first and last letters of 'ornamental'.
explanation.definitionFit: Olfactory is the adjective relating to the sense of smell.

clue.text: Possibly a butterfly in Lima — good size, too

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A large butterfly spotted in the Peruvian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'limA GOod' after the I; 'size, too' is a tag adding that the hidden word is a good size, and does no wordplay work.
explanation.definitionFit: The imago is the adult winged stage of an insect, which in a butterfly is the familiar form.

clue.text: Drink manufacturer at rest

explanation.surface: A distiller takes a break.
explanation.definitionFit: A still is apparatus for distilling spirits; still also means motionless, not moving.

clue.text: Nonconformist fellow's recalled to team — not out nought!

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the fellow's name is read backwards

parts.note: Sid is a typical man's name standing for any fellow
a side is a team in sport

indicators.note: out signals that nought is removed from the word before it

parts.note: taken as written before the deletion
nought is the figure zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A cricketer who went against the grain is brought back into the side, having just been dismissed for a duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not out' and 'nought' sound like cricket scores; 'out' removes O (nought) from NOT, giving NT, and 'recalled' turns SID into DIS. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissident is someone who dissents from established views or authority.

clue.text: Paid for way I write a journal

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
to pen something is to write it
a diary is a daily journal

explanation.surface: A writer is being paid to keep a regular diary.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipendiary receives a stipend, a fixed salary, rather than being unpaid.

clue.text: Semblance of truth aimed at by Pooh-Bah's corroborative detail

definitions.text: aimed at by Pooh-Bah's corroborative detail

explanation.surface: A theatrical character fakes credibility with invented particulars.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Mikado, Pooh-Bah offers 'merely corroborative detail, intended to give artistic' realism to a 'bald and unconvincing narrative'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the appearance of being real or true, which Pooh-Bah's invented details were meant to lend his story.

clue.text: Emptiness gets us wandering' into first-class inn

indicators.note: wandering means straying about, so the letters drift into a new order

parts.note: A1 is a mark meaning first-class, read as the letters A and I
taken as written

explanation.surface: We find ourselves aimlessly drifting into a top-rate hotel, feeling hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a link but is part of the pool: INTO, AI and INN are rearranged together. 'gets us' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanition is exhaustion and emptiness from lack of nourishment.

clue.text: Feelings of doubt familiar to apothecaries?

explanation.surface: Old pharmacists know all about moral hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: Scruples are moral qualms; a scruple was also a small apothecaries' weight of twenty grains.

clue.text: It makes the rounds, being useful for drawers

definitions.text: It makes the rounds, being useful for drawers

parts.words: It makes the rounds, being useful for drawers
parts.note: rounds are ammunition, once wrapped in a heavy paper, and drawers are artists, not chests of furniture

explanation.surface: Something that does the rounds and is handy for a chest of drawers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drawers' suggests furniture or underwear but means people who draw; the thick paper was first used to make gun cartridges.
explanation.definitionFit: This heavy rough paper, once used for ammunition cases, is favoured by artists for sketching.

clue.text: Individual wearing frilly collar — an ugly customer!

indicators.note: the individual is wearing the collar, which sits on top of it in this down entry

parts.note: a ruff is a stiff pleated collar
I is the single individual, the first person

explanation.surface: Someone in an Elizabethan collar turns out to be a nasty piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ugly customer' is an idiom for a dangerous person, not someone unattractive in a shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruffian is a violent lawless person, a thug.

clue.text: Try to excel the runner behind

parts.note: the emu is a large flightless bird that runs
late means behind time

explanation.surface: An athlete trailing the field strains to outdo the leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the runner' looks like an athlete but is the flightless bird; 'behind' is LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To emulate is to imitate in an effort to equal or surpass.

clue.text: Rock sounds agreeable to some

indicators.note: sounds signals that the word is said aloud, as some people say it

parts.note: nice means pleasant or agreeable

explanation.surface: A geologist hears that some people find a stone pleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent G makes the rock's name sound like a word for pleasant; 'to some' allows that not everyone says it so.
explanation.definitionFit: Gneiss is a banded metamorphic rock.

clue.text: Cast in nude production is not established

indicators.note: in places the first word inside the reworked letters that follow it
a production of a word makes something new from it, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the four letters are taken as fodder
to cast metal is to found it in a mould

explanation.surface: Actors appear naked in a show, an unproven idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks theatrical beside 'production', but it is the metalworking verb FOUND; 'production' rearranges NUDE into UNDED, around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unfounded lacks a basis, so it is not proven or supported.

clue.text: Excessive, but not yet payable

explanation.surface: A bill that is too high and not even owed yet.
explanation.definitionFit: Undue means unwarranted, excessive; read literally it is not yet owing.

clue.text: Place in vessel for railwaymen in N Ireland on the way back

indicators.note: in places the railway union inside the reversed abbreviation
on the way back means travelling in reverse, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: NI is the abbreviation for Northern Ireland
the NUR was Britain's National Union of Railwaymen

explanation.surface: Railway workers in Northern Ireland are given a vessel on their return journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the way back' turns NI into IN, which then holds NUR.
explanation.definitionFit: To inurn is to put ashes into an urn, a funerary vessel.

clue.text: Shed for animals finally erected for land-owner

parts.note: a lair is a den or resting place for animals, and in Scots also a cattle shed

indicators.note: finally takes only the closing letter of the following word

explanation.surface: A barn for livestock is at last put up for the estate owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erected' looks like an instruction to turn something upward; only its last letter D is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is a Scottish landed proprietor, the owner of an estate.

clue.text: A rich rival nearly wrecked this mock serenade

indicators.note: wrecked means smashed up, so these letters are broken and rebuilt
nearly means not quite all, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before its last letter goes

explanation.surface: A wealthy competitor almost ruined a noisy mocking performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' trims RIVAL to RIVA; 'wrecked' rearranges A RICH RIVA.
explanation.definitionFit: A charivari is a cacophonous din of pans and kettles made to mock newlyweds, a rough mocking serenade.

clue.text: Eccentric Scotsman seen climbing

indicators.note: climbing in a down clue means reading upward, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: Mac, from the common surname prefix, is a nickname for a Scotsman

explanation.surface: An odd Scot is spotted scaling a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentric' looks like an adjective but is a noun: an eccentric wheel in engineering.
explanation.definitionFit: A cam is an eccentric, a rotating projection converting circular motion to reciprocating movement.

clue.text: Ray makes a star smile broadly

parts.note: the sun is our nearest star
to beam is to give a wide smile

explanation.surface: A man named Ray makes a celebrity grin widely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ray' poses as a man's name but means a beam of light.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaft of sunlight is a single beam of light from the sky.

clue.text: Where in America to use a lot of time without hesitation

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the long period surrounds the pause

parts.note: yonks is British slang for a very long time
er is the sound of a speaker hesitating

explanation.surface: A traveller asks where in the States to spend ages without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside; YONKS is British slang for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Yonkers is a city in New York State, just north of the Bronx.
